titulo: German medical students' learning environment during the fading COVID-19 pandemic
resumo: BACKGROUND: The Medical School's learning environment (MSLE) is important for medical students' academic performance and mental well-being. COVID-19 disrupted medical education worldwide through restrictions on practical and in-person teaching. Although several studies have showcased the immediate effects on medical students' perceptions of MSLE and mental well-being, less is known about the changes during the transition to post-pandemic medical education. METHODS: Four cross-sectional online surveys were conducted at a German medical school between winter 2021/2022 and summer 2023. MSLE was assessed using three items from the Johns Hopkins Learning Environment Scale (JHLES) and three self-developed items. Various validated items assessed distress (DT), perceived stress (PSS-4), depression (PHQ-2), anxiety (GAD-2), and loneliness (R-UCLA-3). Analyses included group comparisons and binary logistic regression. RESULTS: Across four survey waves, 687 individual medical and dental students participated. resumo: BACKGROUND: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has significantly affected the mental health of university students. However, differences in mental health and coping styles across pandemic-related periods remain insufficiently understood. Although coping styles have been associated with depressive symptoms, it remains unclear whether these associations differ across pandemic-related periods among students with subthreshold depressive symptoms, a high-risk group for clinical depression. This study examined differences in depressive symptoms, disordered eating behaviors, and coping styles across pandemic-related periods, with a particular focus on the association between coping styles and depressive symptoms among students with subthreshold depressive symptoms. Persistent high anxiety levels may be contextually linked to an accumulation of concurrent global challenges, including climate change and geopolitical conflicts, that have been described as a “polycrisis” and are characterized by pervasive uncertainty. However, this framework was not directly examined in the present study. abnt: MARCHI, A.; MEDA, N.; PARDINI, S. et al. SADIE: a longitudinal Survey on Anxiety, Depression, Internalising and Externalising symptoms in Italian university students - a study protocol. **BMJ open**, 2026. DOI: 10.1136/bmjopen-2026-116883.
titulo: SADIE: a longitudinal Survey on Anxiety, Depression, Internalising and Externalising symptoms in Italian university students - a study protocol
resumo: INTRODUCTION: University students experience escalating academic, social and financial stress, resulting in high prevalence of anxiety (18%-40%), depression (12-35%) and burnout (20-30%). The COVID-19 pandemic intensified these issues, but most studies report symptom remission post-lockdown, highlighting the need for long-term prospective data on symptom trajectories and risk factors. Participants will complete online assessments via REDCap at baseline, 6-month, 18-month and 36-month follow-ups. titulo: The MAPme Project: Implementing a College-Based Study of Substance Use and Mental Wellness
resumo: BACKGROUND: Transitional age youth aged 18-25 years are more likely to engage in risky behaviors, displaying significantly higher alcohol and illicit drug use levels than adolescents and older adults. titulo: Adapting new norms: A mixed-method study exploring mental well-being challenges in dental technology education
resumo: BACKGROUND: The present study, grounded in the Stress-Adaptation-Growth theory, aims to explore the mental well-being among dental technology students during the post-pandemic period. abnt: JACOBS, E. J.; SPIKER, S.; NEWSOME, K. B. et al. Mental health in undergraduate students several months into the COVID-19 pandemic compared to before the pandemic. **Journal of American college health : J of ACH**, 2025. DOI: 10.1080/07448481.2023.2277193.
titulo: Mental health in undergraduate students several months into the COVID-19 pandemic compared to before the pandemic
resumo: OBJECTIVE: To compare mental health indicators among undergraduates in Fall 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, and Fall 2020, when many students returned to campus amidst restrictions on in-person contact. PARTICIPANTS: Analyses included 26,881 undergraduate students, aged 18-24, from 70 U.S. institutions. METHODS: Students completed the National College Health Assessment-III survey in Fall 2019 or Fall 2020. RESULTS: The prevalences of high stress, loneliness, a low flourishing score, and serious psychological distress increased in 2020 compared to 2019. Serious psychological distress increased substantially in 2020 among students not living with family (adjusted prevalence ratio (aPR)=1.36, 95% CI 1.29-1.45) but not among students living with family (aPR = 1.09, 95% CI 0.95-1.26). CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest prevalences of several indicators of poor mental health were elevated among U.S. undergraduates several months into the pandemic. The pandemic may have had greater impact on mental health among students not living with family.

abnt: JAMIESON, J. Why self-care and mentorship are vital for college students. **Journal of American college health : J of ACH**, 2025. DOI: 10.1080/07448481.2023.2269420.
titulo: Why self-care and mentorship are vital for college students
resumo: College is a big adjustment for students, and it doesn't come without its challenges, including being in a new place with new responsibilities. It is a stressful time that presents new obstacles and frustrations that can lead to increased anxiety, depression, and mental health challenges. As students engage on campus and return to in-person classes, it is vital for university faculty to create activities that promote positive thinking and increase self-confidence in these young learners. Faculty mentorship combined with the development of self-care activities are vital techniques to train students how to cope effectively throughout college and life.

titulo: Responding to extreme stress: Resilience and psychological distress in undergraduate nursing students in the Western Cape, South Africa
resumo: BACKGROUND: Nursing students face significant academic and clinical stressors that can affect their psychological well-being. OBJECTIVES: This study investigated psychological distress and resilience among junior (1st year - 2nd year) and senior (3rd year - 4th year) undergraduate nursing students exposed to a major stressor at two universities in the Western Cape, South Africa. Measures include psychological distress (Kessler-10), resilience (Response to Stressful Experiences Scale) and fear of COVID-19 (Fear of COVID-19 Scale). titulo: Mental health patterns and associated social determinants among university and college students in sub-Saharan Africa during the COVID-19 pandemic era: a scoping review
resumo: Background: Evidence on student mental health in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) remains limited, particularly studies examining how mental health patterns intersect with social determinants within higher education institutions (HEIs). This scoping review identifies gaps in the literature documenting student mental health and associated social determinants during the COVID-19 period and highlights priorities for future research in SSA. Methods: Eight databases (MEDLINE, PsycInfo, Open Access Journals, CINAHL, Google Scholar, Cochrane Library, ProQuest, Scopus) and grey literature were searched for English-language studies from 2020 to 2023. Sixty-seven studies from 214 full-text articles screened met the inclusion criteria. Results: The included studies varied widely in their examination of student mental health and its links to social determinants of health (SDOH). resumo: BACKGROUND: Mental disorders impose a substantial burden on college students, and prevention has become a public health priority. Regular physical activity is extensively recognized as advantageous for mental health, but current evidence primarily focuses on the dose of exercise while overlooking the role of exercise patterns (such as regularity) and their potential biological processes. The inflammatory hypothesis of mental disorders offers a theoretical framework for this, yet the temporal association between behavioral regularity, inflammatory dynamics, and psychological risk remains unknown. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to examine whether objectively measured exercise regularity, assessed using wearable devices, was associated with the risk of new-onset mental disorders in college students and whether systemic inflammation, indexed by hs-CRP and IL-6, partially mediated this association. titulo: Joint associations of sleep duration and screen time with mental health symptoms among 10,620 Chinese university students: An exploratory cross-sectional dose-response analysis
resumo: BACKGROUND: Psychological distress is common among university students and is associated with modifiable lifestyle factors. This study examined the joint associations of sleep duration and screen time with mental health symptoms and explored whether physical activity (PA) dose-response patterns varied across sleep-screen profiles. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 10,620 Chinese university students (mean age 19.8 ± 1.3 years). Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline models were used to estimate associations and explore dose-response patterns. RESULTS: Prevalence rates were 43.7% for depression, 40.7% for anxiety, and 17.6% for stress symptoms. resumo: BACKGROUND: International students may experience psychological challenges associated with migration, academic demands, and adjustment to a new cultural environment. Although previous research has documented mental health concerns in this population, less is known about the relationships among migration-related factors, perceived stress, and mental health outcomes within specific UK higher-education settings. METHODS: A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted among international students enrolled at the University of Wolverhampton. Data were collected using an online questionnaire that included demographic information, migration-related variables, the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale (DASS-21), and a measure of perceived mental stress. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise participants' characteristics and mental health outcomes. titulo: Post-secondary Student Mental Health During COVID-19: A Meta-Analysis
resumo: The COVID-19 pandemic has posed notable challenges to post-secondary students, causing concern for their psychological well-being. In the face of school closures, academic disruptions, and constraints on social gatherings, it is crucial to understand the extent to which mental health among post-secondary students has been impacted in order to inform support implementation for this population. The present meta-analysis examines the global prevalence of clinically significant depression and anxiety among post-secondary students during the COVID-19 pandemic. Several moderator analyses were also performed to examine sources of variability in depression and anxiety prevalence rates. resumo: The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health of students in locked-down colleges remains obscure. titulo: Resilience amid Academic Stress: The Moderating Impact of Social Support among Social Work Students
resumo: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between academic stress and perceived resilience among social work students, and to identify social support as a protective factor of resilience on this relationship. titulo: Coping with academic stress: Ambiguity and uncertainty tolerance in college students
resumo: Stress is a barrier to academic success for college students and the unique resilience effects of ambiguity and uncertainty tolerance have yet to be explored. We hypothesized that tolerance of ambiguity and tolerance of uncertainty relate to academic stress differently. We recruited 158 undergraduate participants from a medium-size public university in the Midwestern United States. Participants completed measures of ambiguity tolerance, uncertainty tolerance, and academic stress coping strategies. Three separate regression analyses were conducted to predict approach coping, avoidance coping, and social support coping. Results indicated that intolerance of ambiguity is a stronger predictor of approach and avoidance academic stress coping strategies compared to intolerance of uncertainty. These findings will allow for a better understanding of the dynamics underlying coping with academic stress that will be helpful to consider in vocational as well as mental health counseling for college students.
